answer: The papers were not provided, so I am assuming paper3 is DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014) and paper2 is node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016). Under that assumption, paper3's SkipGram uses hierarchical softmax when computing the softmax over the full vertex vocabulary is too expensive. Hierarchical softmax replaces the flat softmax with a binary tree over vertices, so each prediction costs roughly O(log |V|) instead of O(|V|). Node2vec motivates a different neighborhood design because a fixed neighborhood, such as DeepWalk's uniform random walk, mixes two kinds of similarity. Breadth-first exploration captures structural equivalence, so nodes with similar local roles are embedded together. Depth-first exploration captures homophily, so nodes in the same community are embedded together. Node2vec therefore uses a biased second-order random walk with return parameter p and in-out parameter q to interpolate between BFS-like and DFS-like sampling, and it can be tuned for communities, roles, or both.
